cues.text: Welcome to the targeted NEET Chemistry closeout, using an AI generated Marin
voice.
The first topic makes the calcium carbide route to ethyne explicit.
The balanced equation is calcium carbide plus two water molecules giving one
ethyne molecule and one calcium hydroxide formula unit.
In formulas, calcium C two plus two H two O gives C two H two plus
calcium O H taken twice.
One mole of calcium carbide therefore corresponds ideally to one mole of
ethyne, assuming the stated reaction and complete conversion.
That is a stoichiometric comparison rather than an experimental procedure.
Existing organic halogen chapter nineteen explains how two eliminations from a
suitable vicinal dihalide can produce an alkyne, so that material should be
reused rather than called missing.
Carbon chain construction by an acetylide is another different transformation
already discussed in the hydrocarbon class.
Distinguish hydrolysis of carbide, elimination from a dihalide and carbon
carbon bond formation.
None of those names alone establishes an observed yield or the purity of a
collected material.
Alkyne polymerisation needs its own comparison rather than being inferred only
from the existing ethene polymer example.
In ideal linear polymerisation of ethyne, the repeat unit is C H double bond C
H along a conjugated chain, usually called polyacetylene.
Each incorporated ethyne unit retains two carbon and two hydrogen atoms in the
ideal atom inventory.
Ignoring end groups, one hundred units therefore contain two hundred carbon
atoms and two hundred hydrogen atoms.
This differs from polyethene, whose repeat unit contains four hydrogens for
every two carbons.
A separate textbook reaction combines three ethyne molecules to give one
benzene molecule, described as cyclic polymerisation or cyclotrimerisation.
The atom balance is three times C two H two giving C six H six.
This is one six membered aromatic ring rather than a long polyacetylene chain.
Appropriate reaction conditions determine which chemical transformation is
described; this lesson states the molecular comparison without giving a
preparation protocol.
Equal total composition does not make chain connectivity and ring connectivity
identical.
The older textbook Freon comparison commonly uses Freon twelve,
dichlorodifluoromethane, with formula C Cl two F two.
It is a chlorofluorocarbon, or C F C.
Such compounds had important refrigerant and aerosol propellant applications
because of useful physical properties and relative stability near the surface.
That stability also allows some emissions to persist and reach the
stratosphere.
There, energetic ultraviolet radiation can release chlorine containing
reactive
species, and catalytic reaction cycles can remove ozone.
A catalyst like chlorine species can be regenerated, so one released chlorine
atom is not necessarily limited to destroying one ozone molecule.
Stratospheric ozone depletion increases concern about ultraviolet exposure at
the surface; it is not the same physical mechanism as greenhouse warming.
Some compounds can be relevant to both issues through different properties.
Freon is a commercial family name, so avoid claiming that every refrigerant or
every compound sold under a related label contains chlorine and follows the
identical ozone mechanism.
Use the specified molecular example and distinguish historical uses from
current product or regulatory advice.
The existing hydrocarbon class explains ethane in a Newman view.
This chapter adds the required sawhorse comparison.
A Newman projection looks directly along the carbon carbon bond.
The nearer carbon is represented by the central point and the farther carbon
by
a circle, with three hydrogen directions associated with each carbon.
A sawhorse drawing views the same bond obliquely, showing the two carbon
positions joined by a sloping bond and three attached hydrogens at each end.
Keep the front and rear carbon assignments consistent when moving between
drawings.
In staggered ethane, the nearest front and rear carbon hydrogen directions
have
a sixty degree dihedral angle; in an eclipsed arrangement they align at zero
degrees.
The staggered conformation has lower torsional energy in the introductory
comparison.
Rotation changes conformation without changing which atoms are bonded, so
these
pictures are not different constitutional isomers.
A drawing's apparent angle on a flat page is not automatically the actual
spatial bond angle.
Compare the relative hydrogen directions around the selected carbon carbon
axis.
Transition elements occur in nature in several chemical forms rather than as a
collection of isolated neutral atoms.
Many occur in oxide or sulfide minerals, while some metals can also occur in
native form under suitable geological conditions.
A mineral is a naturally occurring substance with a characteristic composition
and structure.
Calling a deposit an ore adds a resource and extraction context; economic
usefulness is not fixed by an elemental symbol alone.
Familiar oxide examples include hematite, iron two O three, and magnetite,
iron
three O four.
Chromite has formula iron chromium two O four, while pyrolusite is associated
with manganese dioxide.
Existing d and f block chapters eleven and thirteen connect chromium and
manganese compounds with the preparation chemistry of the prescribed oxidants.
These occurrence examples do not imply that every transition metal has one
identical mineral source or one oxidation state.
For chromite, assigning iron plus two and oxygen minus two gives chromium plus
three in the elementary formula ledger.
Mineral identity and metallic properties remain different questions.
The existing oxygen compound recording emphasizes structures and reactions.
Add a few representative applications to connect those properties with uses.
Ethanol is used as a solvent and fuel and is also the alcohol in alcoholic
beverages.
Methanol also has solvent, fuel and industrial feedstock roles, but it is
toxic
and is not an interchangeable beverage ingredient.
Diethyl ether is a volatile solvent and a historical anaesthetic example,
while
acetone is a familiar ketone solvent.
Their usefulness depends on properties and context, not merely on all
containing oxygen.
Phenol and formaldehyde participate in important resin chemistry, illustrating
a synthetic material application.
Acetic acid is an industrial chemical and a constituent of vinegar at an
appropriate dilute food formulation; that statement does not make concentrated
laboratory acid equivalent to a food product.
These are representative uses within the general syllabus heading, not a new
list of required manufacturing processes.
In an examination comparison, name the compound and the relevant property
rather than claiming that every member of one functional group has identical
uses or biological effects.
Phenol sulphonation completes the named electrophilic substitution comparison
alongside the existing bromination and nitration explanations.
The hydroxyl group activates the aromatic ring and directs substitution mainly
towards ortho and para sites in the elementary account.
The introduced group is sulfonic acid, S O three H, attached through sulfur to
a ring carbon.
The original ring hydroxyl group is retained.
This is different from merely drawing a sulfate ester on the phenolic oxygen.
In the familiar concentrated sulfuric acid comparison, cooler conditions favor
the ortho hydroxybenzenesulfonic acid product, while the warmer comparison
favors the para product.
Reversibility and the stated conditions matter, so this should not be turned
into a claim that every sample contains one perfectly pure isomer.
The existing hydrocarbon sulfonation chapter already explains the broader
reversible substitution framework.
Here the missing connection is the phenol substrate and its directed products.
In a structure question, mark the original hydroxyl carbon first, then locate
the new sulfonic acid group relative to it.
Alkyne addition requires tracking how many pi bonds remain after each step.
Under the usual ionic textbook comparison, adding one equivalent of hydrogen
bromide to propyne gives mainly two bromopropene, a vinyl bromide with one
carbon carbon double bond remaining.
A second equivalent gives the familiar geminal dibromide, two two
dibromopropane, with both bromines on the same carbon.
The first and second products are therefore not the same functional class.
This is a stated ordinary ionic pathway; the peroxide effect should not be
generalized to every hydrogen halide or reaction context.
Adding bromine itself is another comparison: one equivalent can give a
dibromoalkene, while further addition can give a tetrabromoalkane.
The reagent supplies two bromine atoms per bromine molecule rather than one
hydrogen and one bromine.
Existing hydrocarbon chapters six and nine already explain hydrogenation and
hydration, including ethyne's aldehyde exception.
Combine those lessons with this equivalents ledger, and check every carbon,
hydrogen and halogen count before selecting a product.
A homologous series groups compounds with a common structural pattern and
functional group, where successive ordinary members differ by a C H two unit.
Methanol, ethanol and the propanol members illustrate the simple saturated
monohydric alcohol series.
Their formulas progress from C H four O to C two H six O to C three H eight O.
The relative formula mass increases by about fourteen for each such step using
carbon twelve and hydrogen one.
Comparable functional groups support related chemical reaction types, but
boiling points, solubility and other physical properties can change with chain
length.
Members need not be structural isomers because their molecular formulas
differ.
Conversely, propan one ol and propan two ol have the same molecular formula
and
are positional isomers, not two successive fourteen unit steps.
A general formula also needs a structural scope: a saturated open chain
monohydric alcohol comparison is not a formula for every oxygen compound, ring
or unsaturated molecule.
Identify the functional pattern before using a homologous series rule.
The existing mole class teaches mass combination laws and equal gas amounts at
equal temperature and pressure.
Complete the connection with Gay Lussac's law of combining gas volumes: gases
participating in a suitable reaction have simple whole number volume ratios
when compared at the same temperature and pressure.
In the idealized hydrogen oxygen example, two volumes of hydrogen react with
one volume of oxygen to form two volumes of water vapor, with all volumes
referred to the same conditions and the product remaining gaseous.
Thus four litres of hydrogen and two litres of oxygen correspond ideally to
four litres of water vapor at that common reference condition.
If the water condenses, its liquid volume is not four litres by this gas ratio
argument.
Avogadro's equal volume comparison connects these ratios with relative
molecule
counts and balanced coefficients.
Do not compare one hot reactant volume with a cold product volume without
correcting the conditions.
State the physical phase as carefully as the numerical ratio.
